title: One sheet in the way
hook: Three kinds of radiation hit one sheet of paper. Which ones get through?

knows: that radioactive atoms decay and give off radiation
doesNotKnow: that alpha, beta and gamma are stopped by very different amounts of material
that the heaviest radiation is the easiest to stop

misconception: All radiation passes through everything, or alpha is the most penetrating because it is the heaviest.
objective: The learner can say that a sheet of paper stops alpha almost entirely, a few millimetres of aluminium stop beta, and gamma needs thick lead to be cut a lot, because heavy charged radiation gives up its energy quickly.

claims.text: Alpha radiation is helium nuclei, beta radiation is fast electrons, and gamma radiation is high-energy light.
claims.source: IAEA / US NRC radiation basics; Atkins, Chemical Principles (types of radioactive decay). Beta here means beta-minus.

claims.text: A sheet of paper stops alpha particles almost entirely.
claims.source: US NRC 'Types of radiation' and IAEA radiation basics: alpha is stopped by a sheet of paper or the outer layer of skin. Alpha range in air about 5 cm for 5 MeV.

claims.text: Beta radiation is stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium; about 3 mm stops a beta of about 1 MeV.
claims.source: US NRC / IAEA: beta is stopped by a thin sheet of aluminium. Range of a 1 MeV electron in aluminium about 0.4 g/cm² / 2.7 g/cm³ = 1.5 mm (NIST ESTAR), so 3 mm stops it.

claims.text: Most beta rays pass through a sheet of paper (about 95 in 100 in this model).
claims.source: Paper is about 0.008 g/cm² (80 g/m²) against a 1 MeV beta range of about 0.4 g/cm² (NIST ESTAR); stage count 95 is a rounded illustration, not a measurement.

claims.text: Gamma rays pass through paper and 3 mm of aluminium almost unchanged (about 100 and about 95 in 100).
claims.source: Narrow-beam attenuation I/I0 = exp(−(μ/ρ)·ρ·x); 1 MeV photons, aluminium μ/ρ 0.0613 cm²/g, ρ 2.70 g/cm³, x 0.3 cm gives 0.95 (NIST XCOM). Rounded.

claims.text: Even 5 cm of lead leaves about 2 in 100 gamma rays of 1 MeV; thick lead reduces gamma a lot but does not stop it completely.
claims.source: Lead μ/ρ 0.0710 cm²/g at 1 MeV, ρ 11.35 g/cm³, x 5 cm: exp(−4.03) = 0.018 (NIST XCOM), about 2 in 100. Narrow beam, ignores scattered rays.

claims.text: Model: each source sends 100 rays per second; the counts are rounded illustrations for about 5 MeV alpha and 1 MeV beta and gamma.
claims.source: Stage caption '100 rays per second from each source; counts are about'. Energy dependence: other energies stop differently.

claims.text: Alpha particles give up their energy in the first bit of matter they meet because they are heavy and charged; neutral gamma goes deep.
claims.source: Bethe stopping power grows with charge squared; photons have no charge (Knoll, Radiation Detection and Measurement, ch. 2). IAEA radiation basics.

recall.question: Which is stopped most easily by a thin barrier like paper or skin?
options: none of them can be stopped
recall.why: Alpha particles are heavy and charged, so they lose their energy within the first thin layer; gamma needs thick lead or concrete to be reduced much.
